For $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, let $n:=k/|k|$ and let the complex
transverse fibre be
$T_k:=\{v\in\mathbb C^3:\sum_j k_jv_j=0\}$. On $\mathbb C^3$ define
$C(k)v:=i\,n\times v$ and
$P_T(k)v:=v-n\sum_j n_jv_j$. Define
$P_\sigma(k):=\tfrac12(P_T(k)+\sigma C(k))$ for $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$.
Use the Hermitian product
$\langle u,v\rangle_H:=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j$. Then $P_T(k)$ is the
orthogonal projection onto $T_k$; $C(k)$ is Hermitian, vanishes on the
longitudinal line, and satisfies $C(k)^2=P_T(k)$. The restrictions of
$P_{+1}(k)$ and $P_{-1}(k)$ to $T_k$ are orthogonal rank-one projections with
sum $P_T(k)$. Their ranges are the two helicity eigenspaces, with eigenvalues
$+1$ and $-1$ for $C(k)$.

Here $k$ is a spatial wavevector with units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $|k|$ is its
Euclidean norm, $t$ is in seconds, and $i^2=-1$; thus the phase is
dimensionless and real part is taken componentwise.
If $a$ carries units $\mathrm{T\,m^4}$, then $A$ carries $\mathrm{T\,m}$,
$E$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $B$ carries $\mathrm T$. These fields are
real and jointly smooth on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; at each fixed time
$A,E,B$ are Schwartz functions of $x$, and their spatial Schwartz seminorms are
bounded on every compact time interval. They satisfy the smooth source-free
vacuum Maxwell equations and the Coulomb condition
$\operatorname{div}A=0$ with the stated scalar potential $\varphi=0$. Their
total field energy
$W(t):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{[-R,R]^3}u(x,t)\,d^3x$, with $u$ the vacuum
energy density, is finite for every $t$. The amplitudes are a classical Fourier
description; no photon state is defined.

Let $V=\mathbb R^4$ with ordered coframe $e^0=dx^0,e^1=dx^1,e^2=dx^2,e^3=dx^3$, bilinear form $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, inverse $\eta^{-1}=\eta$, and volume form $\mathrm{vol}_\eta=e^0\wedge e^1\wedge e^2\wedge e^3$. For $0\le k\le4$, give $\Lambda^kV^*$ the induced bilinear pairing $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{\mu_1\cdots\mu_k}\beta^{\mu_1\cdots\mu_k}$, with indices raised by $\eta^{-1}$. The Lorentzian Hodge star is the unique linear map $\star_\eta:\Lambda^kV^*\to\Lambda^{4-k}V^*$ satisfying $\alpha\wedge\star_\eta\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta\,\mathrm{vol}_\eta$ for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^kV^*$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, write $e^I$ for the corresponding wedge, $I^c$ for its increasing complement, $s(I,I^c)$ for the sign of the concatenation $(I,I^c)$ relative to $(0,1,2,3)$, and $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$, where $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. The equivalent basis formula is $\star_\eta e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$.
For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.
$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

An orientation of an $n$-manifold is a smooth choice of a ray in $\det T_pM$ for every $p$. For $n>0$, a chart is oriented when its coordinate frame is in that ray. For $n=0$, the datum is a sign at each point; the unique empty frame does not encode both choices.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.
$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

For $\omega\in\Omega^k(M)$, define the candidate $d\omega$ on smooth vector fields by $$d\omega(X_0,\ldots,X_k)=\sum_i(-1)^iX_i\omega(X_0,\widehat X_i,\ldots,X_k)+\sum_{i<j}(-1)^{i+j}\omega([X_i,X_j],X_0,\widehat X_i,\widehat X_j,\ldots,X_k).$$ The next lemma proves that this candidate is a form.

derivations.claim: The six graph charts in the Definition are smooth coordinate charts on open hemispheres and cover $S^2$; their square-root transition formulas are smooth on overlaps. The outward tangent orientation ray is smooth by the nonvanishing normal $n$, with ambient spatial orientation fixed in [F3] and orientation-ray convention [F5]. By [F1], each $P_\sigma(n)$ is a smooth rank-one projection, so each fibre is a complex line. [F2] identifies the physical direction index with a nonzero SI wavevector normalized to unit length. At any $n_0$, choose a fixed $w\in\mathbb C^3$ with $P_\sigma(n_0)w\ne0$, which exists because the projection has nonzero range. Continuity makes $P_\sigma(n)w\ne0$ on a neighborhood of $n_0$, and $P_\sigma(n)w/\|P_\sigma(n)w\|$ is a smooth unit local section there. This proves local triviality without choosing a frame family over the whole sphere.

The coordinate vectors satisfy $n\cdot e_\theta=n\cdot e_\phi=e_\theta\cdot e_\phi=0$, $\|e_\theta\|=\|e_\phi\|=1$, and $n\times e_\theta=e_\phi$, $n\times e_\phi=-e_\theta$, by the coordinate formulas in [F4]. Hence $v_\sigma^\dagger v_\sigma=1$, $P_Tv_\sigma=v_\sigma$, and $C_nv_\sigma=\sigma v_\sigma$. Substitution gives $P_\sigma v_\sigma=v_\sigma$, so this is a unit local frame of the stated fibre.

For a smooth section $s$ on a chart, define $
abla s:=P_\sigma d s$. Since $P_\sigma s=s$, this is again $L_\sigma$-valued. For every smooth scalar $f$, the product rule gives $
abla(fs)=P_\sigma(df\,s+f\,ds)=df\,s+f
abla s$, so $
abla$ is a connection on the line bundle. In a unit frame $v$, writing $s=a v$ gives $
abla s=(da+a v^\dagger dv)v=(da-iAa)v$ because $A=i v^\dagger dv$.

Differentiating $\langle v,v\rangle_H=1$ gives $2\operatorname{Re}(\sum_j\overline{v_j}\,d v_j)=0$, so $A=i\sum_j\overline{v_j}\,d v_j$ is real-valued. Under $v'=e^{i\chi}v$, direct differentiation gives $v'^\dagger d v'=i\,d\chi+v^\dagger dv$, hence $A'=i v'^\dagger d v'=A-d\chi$. This verifies the declared local gauge transformation and completes the definition of the local connection and curvature conventions.

For $u,v\in\mathbb C^3$, extend the real Euclidean dot and right-handed cross products complex-bilinearly, with coordinate formulas
$$u\cdot v:=\sum_{j=1}^3u_jv_j,\qquad u\times v:=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\ u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\ u_1v_2-u_2v_1).$$
The dot product in these formulas uses no complex conjugation; it differs from the Hermitian product $\langle u,v\rangle_H:=\sum_{j=1}^3\overline{u_j}v_j$. Write $\|z\|_H:=\sqrt{\langle z,z\rangle_H}$ for the associated nonnegative norm on $\mathbb C^3$.

Let $S^2:=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:n\cdot n=1\}$ with the smooth structure given by the six graph charts solving $n_j=\pm\sqrt{1-\sum_{k\ne j}n_k^2}$ on the hemispheres $\pm n_j>0$. Orient it outward using the ordered spatial basis $x^1,x^2,x^3$. Its tangent plane is $T_nS^2=\{X\in\mathbb R^3:n\cdot X=0\}$. Physically, $n=k/|k|$ for a nonzero spatial wavevector $k$ in the SI Fourier description, where $k$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$; hence $n$ is dimensionless and the radial magnitude is discarded. For $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$, set $C_nz:=i\,n\times z$, $P_T(n)z:=z-n(n\cdot z)$, and $P_\sigma(n):=\tfrac12(P_T(n)+\sigma C_n)$ on $\mathbb C^3$. Define the helicity fibre $L_\sigma(n):=\operatorname{range}P_\sigma(n)$ and the total space $L_\sigma:=\{(n,z):n\in S^2,\ z\in L_\sigma(n)\}$, projected to $S^2$ by $(n,z)\mapsto n$.

For an open set $U\subseteq S^2$, a unit frame of $L_\sigma$ over $U$ is a smooth map $v:U\to\mathbb C^3$ such that $v(n)\in L_\sigma(n)$ and $\langle v(n),v(n)\rangle_H=1$ for every $n\in U$. Since each fibre is a complex line, this vector spans that fibre. A local unit frame is such a map on an open neighborhood in $S^2$; a global unit frame is one defined on all of $S^2$.

Fibrewise addition and scalar multiplication are inherited from $\mathbb C^3$. A unit frame $v$ gives the local trivialization $(n,a)\mapsto(n,a v(n))$ from $U\times\mathbb C$ to $L_\sigma|_U$, with inverse $(n,z)\mapsto(n,\langle v(n),z\rangle_H)$. The construction in the Proof supplies such a frame near every $n$, so $L_\sigma$ is a smooth rank-one complex vector subbundle of the product bundle $S^2\times\mathbb C^3\to S^2$, whose projection is $(n,z)\mapsto n$.

On a spherical chart with $0<\theta<\pi$ and a smooth longitude branch $\phi$, write $n=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)$, $e_\theta=(\cos\theta\cos\phi,\cos\theta\sin\phi,-\sin\theta)$, and $e_\phi=(-\sin\phi,\cos\phi,0)$. The local unit helicity frame is $v_\sigma:=(e_\theta+i\sigma e_\phi)/\sqrt2$. For any unit frame $v$ over an open set $U$, write $v^\dagger d v:=\sum_{j=1}^3\overline{v_j}\,d v_j$, where $d v_j$ is the exterior derivative of its $j$th component. Define its Berry connection one-form by $A:=i v^\dagger d v$. A smooth phase change $v'=e^{i\chi}v$, with real smooth $\chi$, changes this local form to $A'=A-d\chi$. The local Berry curvature is the real two-form $F:=dA$ on $U$; no global gluing assertion is made here.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, let
$$C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R^{(S_k^\infty(M))}\quad(k\ge0),\qquad C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=0\quad(k<0),$$
using [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. It is the subspace of [[def-real-singular-chain-complex]] spanned by the smooth simplices, with the same signed face differential.

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].
For every differential form $\omega$, $d(d\omega)=0$.

derivations.claim: In spherical coordinates, $\partial_\theta e_\theta=-n$, $\partial_\theta e_\phi=0$, $\partial_\phi e_\theta=\cos\theta\,e_\phi$, and $\partial_\phi e_\phi=-\cos\theta\,e_\theta-\sin\theta\,n$. Using $e_\theta\cdot e_\theta=e_\phi\cdot e_\phi=1$, $e_\theta\cdot e_\phi=0$, and $e_\theta\cdot n=e_\phi\cdot n=0$, direct expansion gives $v_\sigma^\dagger\partial_\theta v_\sigma=0$ and $v_\sigma^\dagger\partial_\phi v_\sigma=-i\sigma\cos\theta$. Thus $A_\sigma=i v_\sigma^\dagger d v_\sigma=\sigma\cos\theta\,d\phi$.

Differentiating the preceding local form yields $dA_\sigma=-\sigma\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The globally defined form $\omega_{S^2,n}(X,Y)=n\cdot(X\times Y)$ is smooth because its coefficients are polynomial in the embedded coordinates and tangent vectors; since $\partial_\theta n=e_\theta$ and $\partial_\phi n=\sin\theta\,e_\phi$, it satisfies $\omega_{S^2}=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. Therefore $dA_\sigma=-\sigma\omega_{S^2}$ away from the poles. On any overlap neighborhood where two unit frames differ by a smooth real phase $\chi$, [F1] changes $A$ by $-d\chi$, so [F4] gives $dA'=dA$; the local curvatures glue smoothly, and equality with the smooth form $-\sigma\omega_{S^2}$ extends by continuity to the poles.

To compute the flux with [F3], take the boundary $O=\{|x_1|+|x_2|+|x_3|=1\}$ of the unit octahedron. Fix one order of its six vertices. For each of its eight triangular faces, let $\tau_f:\Delta^2\to f$ be the affine simplex using that global vertex order, and compose it with the radial projection $r(x)=x/\|x\|$ to $S^2$. The denominator is nonzero on $O$, so each face map extends smoothly to a neighborhood of its simplex. Give each map coefficient $+1$ or $-1$ so its orientation agrees with the outward sphere orientation. A shared edge then has the same ordered affine edge map in the two adjacent faces and opposite boundary coefficients, so the finite sum $z$ of the eight maps satisfies $\partial z=0$. Each spherical octant has $\omega_{S^2}=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$ and area $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin\theta\,d\theta\int_0^{\pi/2}d\phi=\pi/2$; the eight octants cover the sphere and their edges contribute no two-dimensional integral. Hence $\int_z\omega_{S^2}=8(\pi/2)=4\pi$, and step 2.1 gives $\int_{S^2}F_\sigma:=\int_zF_\sigma=-4\pi\sigma$. Dividing by $2\pi$ gives $-2\sigma$.

Suppose a global smooth unit frame $v$ existed. Then $A=i v^\dagger d v$ would be a global smooth one-form and its curvature would be $F_\sigma=dA$. Applying [F2] to the finite cycle $z$ from step 3.1 gives $\int_zF_\sigma=\int_zdA=\int_{\partial z}A=0$, contradicting $\int_zF_\sigma=-4\pi\sigma\ne0$ by the nonzero values of $\sigma$ in [F1] and step 3.1. Therefore no global smooth unit frame exists.

derivations.claim: For $z\in L_\sigma(n)$, [F2] gives $n\cdot z=0$ and $n\times z=-i\sigma z$. The defining formula therefore reduces to $R_{n,\alpha}z=(\cos\alpha-i\sigma\sin\alpha)z=e^{-i\sigma\alpha}z$. The phase is unchanged when $\alpha$ is increased by $2\pi$ because $\sigma$ is an integer, and addition of angles multiplies phases, proving it is the stated character.

Choose a real unit vector $u\perp n$ and put $v=n\times u$. The real cross-product identities give $|v|=1$, $u\cdot v=0$, and $n\times v=-u$, so $(u,v,n)$ is a positively oriented orthonormal basis. In this basis the real rotation formula has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha&0\\ \sin\alpha&\cos\alpha&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, which is orthogonal with determinant one. Thus $R_{n,\alpha}$ is proper.

Write a section on one chart as $s(t)=a(t)v_j(\gamma(t))$. Since $P_\sigma$ is the orthogonal projection onto the line spanned by the unit vector $v_j$, the projected derivative is $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}s=(\dot a+a\,v_j^\dagger\dot v_j)v_j=(\dot a-iA_j(\dot\gamma)a)v_j$. Thus $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}s=0$ is the scalar ODE $\dot a=iA_j(\dot\gamma)a$, whose solution across that subpath multiplies $a$ by $\exp(i\int A_j)$. derivations.claim: On the punctured cap, the phase change $v_N=e^{i\sigma\phi}v_\sigma$ gives $A_N=A_\sigma-\sigma d\phi=\sigma(\cos\theta-1)d\phi$. Put $x=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$, and $z=\cos\theta$. Since $d\phi=(x\,dy-y\,dx)/(1-z^2)$, this is $A_N=-\sigma(x\,dy-y\,dx)/(1+z)$, which extends smoothly across the north pole because $1+z>0$ there. The rephased frame itself also extends: for $\sigma=+1$ its components are $\frac{1}{2\sqrt2(1+z)}\bigl((1+z)^2-(x+iy)^2,\ i((1+z)^2+(x+iy)^2),\ -2(x+iy)(1+z)\bigr)^T$, and for $\sigma=-1$ they are the complex conjugates. These formulas have nonzero denominator throughout the north patch.

Along the loop, $\oint_\gamma A_N=\int_0^{2\pi}\sigma(\cos\theta_0-1)\,d\phi=-\sigma\Omega$, so [F1] gives $\mathrm{Hol}_\gamma=e^{-i\sigma\Omega}$. Direct integration of the global curvature over the north cap gives $\int_{\Sigma_N}F_\sigma=-\sigma\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\theta_0}\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=-\sigma\Omega$ as well. Thus the cap-flux expression agrees without using the singular spherical gauge at its pole.

In the spherical gauge, $\oint_\gamma A_\sigma=2\pi\sigma\cos\theta_0=-\sigma\Omega+2\pi\sigma$. Since $e^{i2\pi\sigma}=1$ for the integer helicities specified by [F1], exponentiation gives the same holonomy in both gauges.

citations.quote:
For $u,v\in\mathbb C^3$, extend the real Euclidean dot and right-handed cross products complex-bilinearly, with coordinate formulas
$$u\cdot v:=\sum_{j=1}^3u_jv_j,\qquad u\times v:=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\ u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\ u_1v_2-u_2v_1).$$
The dot product in these formulas uses no complex conjugation; it differs from the Hermitian product $\langle u,v\rangle_H:=\sum_{j=1}^3\overline{u_j}v_j$. Write $\|z\|_H:=\sqrt{\langle z,z\rangle_H}$ for the associated nonnegative norm on $\mathbb C^3$.

Let $S^2:=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:n\cdot n=1\}$ with the smooth structure given by the six graph charts solving $n_j=\pm\sqrt{1-\sum_{k\ne j}n_k^2}$ on the hemispheres $\pm n_j>0$. Orient it outward using the ordered spatial basis $x^1,x^2,x^3$. Its tangent plane is $T_nS^2=\{X\in\mathbb R^3:n\cdot X=0\}$. Physically, $n=k/|k|$ for a nonzero spatial wavevector $k$ in the SI Fourier description, where $k$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$; hence $n$ is dimensionless and the radial magnitude is discarded. For $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$, set $C_nz:=i\,n\times z$, $P_T(n)z:=z-n(n\cdot z)$, and $P_\sigma(n):=\tfrac12(P_T(n)+\sigma C_n)$ on $\mathbb C^3$. Define the helicity fibre $L_\sigma(n):=\operatorname{range}P_\sigma(n)$ and the total space $L_\sigma:=\{(n,z):n\in S^2,\ z\in L_\sigma(n)\}$, projected to $S^2$ by $(n,z)\mapsto n$.

For an open set $U\subseteq S^2$, a unit frame of $L_\sigma$ over $U$ is a smooth map $v:U\to\mathbb C^3$ such that $v(n)\in L_\sigma(n)$ and $\langle v(n),v(n)\rangle_H=1$ for every $n\in U$. Since each fibre is a complex line, this vector spans that fibre. A local unit frame is such a map on an open neighborhood in $S^2$; a global unit frame is one defined on all of $S^2$.

Fibrewise addition and scalar multiplication are inherited from $\mathbb C^3$. A unit frame $v$ gives the local trivialization $(n,a)\mapsto(n,a v(n))$ from $U\times\mathbb C$ to $L_\sigma|_U$, with inverse $(n,z)\mapsto(n,\langle v(n),z\rangle_H)$. The construction in the Proof supplies such a frame near every $n$, so $L_\sigma$ is a smooth rank-one complex vector subbundle of the product bundle $S^2\times\mathbb C^3\to S^2$, whose projection is $(n,z)\mapsto n$.

On a spherical chart with $0<\theta<\pi$ and a smooth longitude branch $\phi$, write $n=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)$, $e_\theta=(\cos\theta\cos\phi,\cos\theta\sin\phi,-\sin\theta)$, and $e_\phi=(-\sin\phi,\cos\phi,0)$. The local unit helicity frame is $v_\sigma:=(e_\theta+i\sigma e_\phi)/\sqrt2$. For any unit frame $v$ over an open set $U$, write $v^\dagger d v:=\sum_{j=1}^3\overline{v_j}\,d v_j$, where $d v_j$ is the exterior derivative of its $j$th component. Define its Berry connection one-form by $A:=i v^\dagger d v$. A smooth phase change $v'=e^{i\chi}v$, with real smooth $\chi$, changes this local form to $A'=A-d\chi$. The local Berry curvature is the real two-form $F:=dA$ on $U$; no global gluing assertion is made here.

Fix $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$ and let $L_\sigma(n)$ be the range of the helicity projector $P_\sigma(n)$ over the outward-oriented unit sphere $S^2$. On an angular chart with $0<\theta<\pi$ and a smooth longitude branch $\phi$, use $v_\sigma=(e_\theta+i\sigma e_\phi)/\sqrt2$ and the connection convention $A_\sigma=i v_\sigma^\dagger d v_\sigma$. The spherical frame has Berry one-form $A_\sigma=\sigma\cos\theta\,d\phi$ and curvature $F_\sigma=dA_\sigma=-\sigma\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. If $\omega_{S^2,n}(X,Y):=n\cdot(X\times Y)$ is the outward area form for $X,Y\in T_nS^2$, then this curvature extends smoothly to the whole sphere as $F_\sigma=-\sigma\omega_{S^2}$. Write $\int_{S^2}$ for the outward-oriented integral, evaluated as the sum over the eight radially projected octant triangles described in the Proof. Its total flux is $\int_{S^2}F_\sigma=-4\pi\sigma$, so the flux divided by $2\pi$ is $-2\sigma$ in this convention. The line bundle has no globally smooth unit frame.
